content:
I've just added a space in a (almost) leaf file in a Mathlib PR. Looking at the build step in CI, as expected it only builds the file and the one file that imports it, together with Mathlib.lean. But then it seems to build a lot of Archive and Counterexamples and also many tests. Why is that? Unless there is an import Mathlib at the top of a file (which I don't think is the case), no rebuild should be necessary, as no dependency has changed. (The relevant material is so new that no downstream files in Archive/Counterexamples/Test uses it.)

(Caveat: there are currently problems with github that make all CI steps except building fail. But the cache from the previous build (before adding the space) should still be available.)

If I remember correctly, CI only gets the cache from the base of the PR - not of intermediate PR commits (even if this cache was uploaded). @Bryan Gin-ge Chen mentioned changing this, at some point in the past.

Working on new syntax linters occasionally makes me encounter the extreme version of this: modifying the linter naturally rebuilds all of mathlib (as the linter needs to check all files), but then a merge of master also rebuilds evefything - as opposed to just the new files.
The ping happened to remind me that I should get back to #33044. I guess that may be a different issue though?
That issue (or perhaps some extension, also looking at intermediate commits) might be it!

A further data point: I just submitted a PR that only changes the name of a leaf file. The "build" step in CI still seems to build all the files in MathlibTest (but did not build anything in Archive or Counterexamples). Does this step not check whether the files depend on something that has changed?

Another thing I noticed is that every time CI runs, it seems to build all the tools from scratch. Would it be possible to make it use precompiled versions (as long as the PR does not change anything in the tooling)?

Let me revive this thread (I'd still be interested in an answer to the questions above, BTW; it still looks like CI builds all the tests from scratch) to mention that in a CI run just now I noticed a step "dump declarations and transitive-import counts" (within the Post-Build Step) that took about 2 minutes and which I can't remember having seen before.

  • Is this new?
  • Is it really necessary to spend 2 minutes (I assume that this run was representative in this respect; see here) for whatever it does on every Mathlib CI run?

Thanks, that link helps.

Looking at that run, I think the immediate question may be narrower than the earlier cache discussion: is the dump declarations and transitive-import counts step a recent addition, and is spending about 2 minutes there considered expected for a representative CI run?

If the answer is yes, I’d be interested in understanding what downstream check or workflow depends on it, since that would make it easier to separate intentional post-build cost from accidental rebuild cost.
I added that step as part of a new declaration diff that is lean aware.
Maybe, I should move it to a separate workflow that runs as soon as the cache is available, but is independent of the main build.
(The new declaration diff is not yet working, in case you are wondering: it will take about 4 more steps for that.)

The "build" step in CI still seems to build all the files in MathlibTest (but did not build anything in Archive or Counterexamples). Does this step not check whether the files depend on something that has changed?

I missed this, but the answer is indeed no. If someone can figure out a good way to do this, I'd be happy to review this.

Michael Stoll said:

Another thing I noticed is that every time CI runs, it seems to build all the tools from scratch. Would it be possible to make it use precompiled versions (as long as the PR does not change anything in the tooling)?

I think this might be hard; for example, we need to build Cache to use it to get the cache. Maybe things will change when we switch to lake cache?

Bryan Gin-ge Chen said:

Michael Stoll said:

I missed this, but the answer is indeed no. If someone can figure out a good way to do this, I'd be happy to review this.

What is the difference between building (say) Archive and building the tests?

didn't read the entire thread but if I'm not mistaken lake exe cache does not upload or download oleans from MathlibTest, so they need to be rebuild on every run. I don't think there is any particular reason which would prevent a PR from changing that.

The CI explicitly stages and uploads files for Mathlib, Archive, and Counterexamples.

It's possible that some changes like #35415 would be necessary for lake exe cache get MathlibTest to work, but I think it might just work already (besides the files newer being uploaded in the first place).

Bryan Gin-ge Chen said:

Michael Stoll said:

Another thing I noticed is that every time CI runs, it seems to build all the tools from scratch. Would it be possible to make it use precompiled versions (as long as the PR does not change anything in the tooling)?

I think this might be hard; for example, we need to build Cache to use it to get the cache. Maybe things will change when we switch to lake cache?

I think how this would work is that the tools could move to the mathlib-ci repo which could build them and provide them somehow., The CI scripts in mathlib could then call the built executables directly without rebuilding them. For tools lying inside the mathlib4/ repo, I think you won't get around rebuilding them from scratch

We fetch them from master in most cases (PRs), so we could build an artifact for every commit to master in another pipeline and then fetch that artifact (or manually publish a version of these tools in mathlib-ci). This step is always ~30s:

I'd say this strategy would save us around 20s for PRs
Decoupling the cache tool from the repo entirely is not possible because we use it as a post-update hook for dependents

Maybe it does make sense to start in parallel the jobs that require the cache, but are not dependent on one another. I'm thinking now of the global linting step and running the tests. The new PR summary could be another one.

I thought about this in the past, but some of these are not exactly lightweight (e.g. linting), so running them on stock GitHub runners makes them a lot slower, and the self-hosted runners are only 10 so hogging "N" for post-build steps seemed unfair

Marcelo Lynch said:

We fetch them from master in most cases (PRs), so we could build an artifact for every commit to master in another pipeline and then fetch that artifact (or manually publish a version of these tools in mathlib-ci).

I'd say this strategy would save us around 20s for PRs

namely #40136

Marcelo Lynch said:

I thought about this in the past, but some of these are not exactly lightweight (e.g. linting), so running them on stock GitHub runners makes them a lot slower, and the self-hosted runners are only 10 so hogging "N" for post-build steps seemed unfair

Still, we could reconsider this. For example, it seems like it's not common to use more than 5/10 machines all at once, so using "one more" per build might still be fine! (The graph shows the count of concurrent jobs in the hoskinsons in the past 14 days)

I just asked Claude to do a simulation for whether splitting test and lint would be worth it and the result was essentially that it wasn't worth it because setting up the runner and downloading the cache takes around 83 seconds and the test step takes 112 seconds so we don't really save that much time (details here).

edit: Actually I just noticed the data only includes runs on branches in the main repo, not forks. Redoing the analysis now with data from branches on forks.

edit 2: after including data from build_fork.yml runs, the conclusion that it wasn't worth it didn't really change.

Could you ask about splitting only test? The rationale would be that test is quicker than lint, so adding the cost of re-downloading might bring it to the same time as lint, but they would run in parallel now, since lint could use the oleans that are available and not be forced to download.
(Right now, lint has to wait for test, so the change would allow lint to run immediately after all the cache settles.)

Also, if it is roughly equal, it might still be worth it, since we may move some of the Post build steps in this process: the separate process would not speed up this step, but would speed up the whole build overall.
(But note it's not possible to 'dispatch' a separate machine while one job is running, so it would need to happen in a different workflow, then collect the results -- kinda awkward, albeit possible)
#40233 is a LLM-generated draft that splits up build along the lines Damiano was thinking; I'll try to review this next week, but anyone should feel free to take a look before then.
#40136 is good to go, by the way -- I tested in ci-dev after merging #40164

Bryan Gin-ge Chen said:

#40233 is a LLM-generated draft that splits up build along the lines Damiano was thinking; I'll try to review this next week, but anyone should feel free to take a look before then.

re: this, note that it should be fine as long as there are idle hoskinsons to pick up the 'split'. But if there is a lot of contention, the workflow might go into the second job and find that all machines are now occupied, and sit there waiting for a hoskinson for a long time, making the end-to-end longer than if everything stayed in the same machine.

Per my graph above it looks like most of the time it should be fine, though.
#40136 is also good if now we're planning on rebuilding the cache tool in even more jobs

I've sent it to bors; one risk I foresee is that needing to pass artifacts around more will make things more fragile because of github flakiness, but I think a 30 second speedup across all jobs makes it worth trying.
if the download fails it falls back to rebuilding
#40233 should now be ready for review / merge. It should help increase the parallelism of the build so when the runners aren't too busy, we should see savings of a few minutes per build.
@Bryan Gin-ge Chen I think the PR description is outdated, and should explain that we're not solely relying on lake exe cache get (which would be expensive!) to move oleans between stages.
Thanks! I've tried to update it to be more accurate.
